title: Map, apply, and vectorize
goal: Choose an appropriate way to transform values and create categories.
prerequisites: You can create columns, filter values, and define a short Python function.

cells.title: Map codes to meaningful labels
cells.explanation: `Series.map()` can look up each value in a dictionary. A code missing from the dictionary produces a missing result. Keep the source codes so you can investigate labels that were not mapped.
cells.code:
codes = pd.Series(["AI", "IT", "CS", None], dtype="string")
labels = {"AI": "Artificial Intelligence", "IT": "Information Technology"}
result = pd.DataFrame({"Code": codes, "Label": codes.map(labels)})
print(result)

questions.prompt: What do the keys of labels represent?
questions.answer: The codes we want to look up.

questions.prompt: Which Label entries will be missing?
questions.answer: The entry for CS, which is not mapped, and the entry whose source code is missing.

questions.prompt: Why should the unmapped CS and missing source code be investigated separately?
questions.answer: One is an observed but unrecognized code; the other was never recorded.

cells.task: For this exercise, define CS as Cybersecurity. Add it to the mapping and rebuild the result while leaving the original missing code missing.
cells.hint: Add one dictionary key-value pair; do not fill every missing label.
cells.solution:
codes = pd.Series(["AI", "IT", "CS", None], dtype="string")
labels = {"AI": "Artificial Intelligence", "IT": "Information Technology", "CS": "Cybersecurity"}
result = pd.DataFrame({"Code": codes, "Label": codes.map(labels)})
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The CS row now has its specified label; the row without a source code remains missing.

check.prompt: What happens to an unmapped key in Series.map with a plain dictionary?
check.feedback: Unlike a general text replacement, a dictionary map returns missing for keys it does not contain.

cells.watch: The meaning of a code must come from a stated codebook, not a guess.
cells.takeaway: Check what a lookup leaves unmatched.

cells.title: Apply a function to each value
cells.explanation: A Python function can express a custom rule for one value. `Series.apply()` calls that function for each entry. When the same rule can be written with built-in column operations, those operations are often simpler and more efficient.
cells.code:
scores = pd.Series([58, 79, 80, 95])
def status(score):
    return "Secure" if score >= 80 else "Review"
result = scores.apply(status)
print(result.tolist())

questions.prompt: What does the function receive each time it is called?
questions.answer: One score value, not the whole Series.

questions.prompt: Which label does a score of exactly 80 receive?
Is apply required for every calculation on a column?
questions.answer: No. Built-in arithmetic, comparisons, string methods, and aggregations often do the job directly.

cells.task: Create the same labels without a custom function. Use a Boolean comparison and a mapping from True/False to labels.
cells.solution:
scores = pd.Series([58, 79, 80, 95])
result = scores.ge(80).map({True: "Secure", False: "Review"})
print(result.tolist())
cells.solution_note: The labels are unchanged. The column comparison makes the threshold visible without a separate function.

check.feedback: ge is the named form of the >= comparison.

cells.watch: These labels use an exercise rule, not an official grading policy.
cells.takeaway: Use a custom function when it adds clarity, not by default.

cells.title: A row function versus column arithmetic
cells.explanation: `DataFrame.apply(..., axis=1)` passes one row at a time to a function. Here Quiz is out of 20 and Project is out of 50, so both must be scaled before weighting them. A direct column formula can express the same calculation.
cells.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({"Quiz": [16, 12, 18], "Project": [40, 35, 45]})
result = df.apply(lambda row: (row["Quiz"] / 20) * 40 + (row["Project"] / 50) * 60, axis=1)
print(result.round(2).tolist())

questions.answer: The function needs Quiz and Project from the same row.

questions.prompt: What is the first weighted percentage?
Why would Quiz + Project be a different measure?
questions.answer: It would sum raw points without the stated 40% and 60% weights.

cells.task: Compute the same weighted percentage with direct column arithmetic, without apply or lambda.
cells.hint: Perform each calculation on the entire df["Quiz"] or df["Project"] Series.
cells.solution_note: The percentages remain 80.0, 66.0, and 90.0. Direct arithmetic also preserves the row index.

check.prompt: With DataFrame.apply, axis=1 passes which object to the function?
check.feedback: axis=1 applies the function across the columns of each row.

cells.watch: Check the maximum points and weights before calculating a percentage.
cells.takeaway: Prefer direct column formulas for ordinary arithmetic.

cells.title: Fixed intervals versus quantile groups
cells.explanation: `cut()` groups numbers using value boundaries that you choose. `qcut()` uses sample quantiles to form groups with roughly similar counts. They answer different questions, and equal-count groups need not have equal numeric widths.
cells.code:
values = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 100])
fixed = pd.cut(values, bins=[0, 50, 100], labels=["Lower", "Upper"], include_lowest=True)
quantile = pd.qcut(values, q=2, labels=["Lower_half", "Upper_half"])
result = pd.DataFrame({"Value": values, "Fixed_band": fixed, "Quantile_band": quantile})
print(result)

questions.prompt: Which method uses the explicit boundary of 50?
How many values are in the lower fixed band and lower quantile group?
questions.answer: Three values are in Lower; two are in Lower_half.

questions.prompt: Why would quantile bands be unsuitable for an official fixed pass threshold?
questions.answer: Their boundaries depend on the current sample rather than a fixed scoring rule.

cells.task: Use students(). Create Score_band using boundaries 0, 60, 80, 100 with labels Developing, Progressing, Secure. Include both 0 and 100, with 60 in Developing and 80 in Progressing. Store the count of each band in a Series named result.
cells.hint: Use cut with right=True and include_lowest=True, then value_counts(sort=False).
cells.solution:
df = students()
df["Score_band"] = pd.cut(df["Score"], bins=[0, 60, 80, 100], labels=["Developing", "Progressing", "Secure"], right=True, include_lowest=True)
result = df["Score_band"].value_counts(sort=False)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The counts are 1 Developing, 5 Progressing, and 6 Secure. These are practice labels with explicit boundary rules.

check.prompt: Which method is appropriate for fixed score boundaries?
check.feedback: cut accepts the exact value boundaries you need.

cells.watch: Tied values can prevent qcut from making the requested number of distinct bins; inspect boundaries and group counts.
cells.takeaway: Choose bands by meaning or by sample distribution, as required.
